title.raw: Anaphylaxis: What to Do After Using an EpiPen
title.rendered: Anaphylaxis: What to Do After Using an EpiPen

content.raw:
If you have just used an epinephrine auto-injector commonly known by the brand name EpiPen or administered one to a loved one, your heart is likely racing. That is a completely normal response, both to the stress of the situation and the medication itself. Using an auto-injector is a brave and necessary move. It is the first line of defense in anaphylaxis treatment, designed to buy you precious time by reversing life-threatening symptoms. However, many people mistakenly believe that once the needle comes out and the symptoms begin to fade, the danger has passed. In reality, the injection is the beginning of the recovery process, not the end. Understanding what comes next is vital for ensuring a full recovery and staying safe from potential "rebound" reactions.

The Moment After: Why Using Your EpiPen Is Only Step One

Epinephrine works quickly to open airways and increase blood pressure, but its effects are temporary. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), epinephrine has a short half-life, meaning it wears off relatively quickly. If the allergen is still in your system, symptoms can return as the medication fades.

Calling 911: Why Professional Medical Help Is Non-Negotiable

The very next step after the injection is calling emergency services. You should always go to the emergency room via ambulance after using epinephrine. Even if you feel "fine" five minutes later, you need professional emergency allergy stabilization. Medical professionals need to monitor your heart rate and oxygen levels and determine if a second dose of epinephrine or other medications, like corticosteroids or antihistamines, are required.

Emergency Allergy Stabilization: What Happens at the Hospital?

When you arrive at the hospital, the medical team’s goal is emergency allergy stabilization. They aren't just checking to see if the first shot worked; they are preparing for what might happen next. The NIH emphasizes that anaphylaxis is a multi-systemic reaction. Doctors will likely:
  • Monitor Vital Signs: Checking your blood pressure and heart rhythm.
  • Administer Fluids: IV fluids may be given if your blood pressure drops significantly.
  • Provide Supplemental Oxygen: To ensure your organs are getting the support they need while your airways recover.
  • Observation: Most patients are kept for 4 to 6 hours to ensure the reaction does not return.

Monitoring for the "Second Wave" of Allergic Reactions

One of the most critical reasons for hospital observation is the "second wave" of allergic reactions, clinically known as biphasic anaphylaxis. As noted by MedlinePlus, up to 20% of people who experience anaphylaxis will have a second reaction hours after the first, even without being re-exposed to the allergen. This second wave can be more severe than the initial episode. Being in a clinical setting when this happens ensures that life-saving intervention is immediate.

Recognizing Red Flags: When a Throat Feels Tight or Breathing Changes

During your recovery, you must stay hyper-aware of your body. Anaphylaxis is a "full-body" event. Even after the initial anaphylaxis treatment, you should watch for these returning symptoms:
  • Respiratory Issues: If your throat feels tight, you develop a hoarse voice, or you experience a persistent cough.
  • Skin Changes: New hives, itching, or sudden paleness.
  • Circulatory Signs: Feeling faint, dizzy, or having a weak, rapid pulse.
  • Gastrointestinal Distress: Severe stomach cramps, vomiting, or diarrhea.
If any of these occur after you have been discharged, treat them as a new emergency and return to the ER immediately.

Immediate Recovery: The First 24 Hours Post-Anaphylaxis

The day after a severe allergic reaction can feel like an "allergy hangover." Your body has just survived a massive inflammatory event and a surge of adrenaline.

Managing Side Effects of Epinephrine

Epinephrine is a synthetic version of the body's natural "fight or flight" hormone. It is common to experience:
  • Shaking or tremors
  • A pounding headache
  • Anxiety or nervousness
  • Nausea
These symptoms generally subside within a few hours as the medication leaves your system. Rest is essential. Avoid strenuous activity and ensure you are in the company of someone who knows your history for at least 24 hours.

Long-Term Safety: Preventing the Next Episode

Once the immediate crisis has passed, it is time to look forward. Prevention is a core part of long-term anaphylaxis treatment.

Restocking and Reviewing Your Action Plan

  • Replace Your Device: An EpiPen is a single-use device. According to the FDA, you should always have at least two unexpired auto-injectors available, as some reactions require a second dose before help arrives.
  • Identify the Trigger: If the cause of the reaction was unknown, schedule an appointment with an allergist for testing.
  • Update Your Plan: Ensure your family, workplace, or school has an updated Allergy Action Plan.

Don't Wait for a "Second Wave": Get Professional Stabilization Now

An EpiPen is a bridge, not a cure. Because the effects of epinephrine are temporary, the risk of a secondary "biphasic" reaction remains high for several hours after your initial symptoms fade. After an EpiPen, you still need emergency monitoring for a possible second-wave (biphasic) reaction. Call 911 or get emergency anaphylaxis care at ER of Irving right away. We are open 24/7. Need immediate care? Call us now at (972) 893-3148 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

How long do I need to stay in the hospital after using an EpiPen? 

Most medical guidelines recommend a minimum observation period of 4 to 6 hours. This is specifically to monitor for a "biphasic" or second-wave reaction.

Can I drive myself to the hospital after an injection? 

No. You should never drive yourself. The symptoms of anaphylaxis can cause dizziness or loss of consciousness suddenly, and the side effects of epinephrine can impair your motor skills. Always call 911.

What if I feel 100% better after the shot? 

Even if you feel completely recovered, the FDA advises seeking emergency medical care immediately. The medication is temporary, and the allergen may still be active in your body.

Why does my throat feel tight even after the hives are gone? 

A tight throat is a sign of airway constriction or swelling (angioedema). This is a high-priority symptom that requires immediate medical evaluation, as it affects your ability to breathe.

Do I need to use a second EpiPen if symptoms don't stop? 

If symptoms do not improve or if they get worse after 5 to 15 minutes, a second injection may be necessary. This is why most patients are prescribed a "two-pack" of auto-injectors.

Will antihistamines like Benadryl stop anaphylaxis? 

No. While antihistamines can help with skin symptoms like hives, they cannot reverse the life-threatening aspects of anaphylaxis, such as low blood pressure or airway closure.

content.raw:

The F.A.S.T. method makes recognition simple enough for anyone to use. This guide covers what a stroke is, how to spot one, what to do in the first 5 minutes, and what happens when you arrive at the ER of Irving.

What is a Stroke? Why Every Minute Counts

A stroke happens when blood flow to part of your brain stops. The brain tissue without blood begins dying within minutes, and the damage spreads fast. Roughly 1.9 million brain cells die every minute during a stroke, according to the American Stroke Association. That is why doctors say "time is brain." The earlier someone gets to an ER, the more brain tissue can be saved. Strokes come in two main forms. An ischemic stroke is caused by a clot blocking a brain artery. A hemorrhagic stroke is caused by a brain artery bursting. Both are emergencies, but they need different treatments at the ER.

The F.A.S.T. Method: 4 Warning Signs of Stroke

The CDC and the American Stroke Association both promote F.A.S.T. as the fastest way to recognize a stroke. Each letter points to one thing to check.
  • F – Face drooping. Ask the person to smile. Does one side of the face droop or feel numb?
  • A – Arm weakness. Ask them to raise both arms. Does one arm drift downward or feel heavy?
  • S – Speech difficulty. Ask them to repeat a simple sentence like "the sky is blue." Are the words slurred or jumbled?
  • T – Time to call 911. Even if symptoms seem to fade, call. Note the exact time symptoms started.
Any one of these signs is enough to call. You do not need all four.

Atypical Stroke Symptoms You Should Not Miss

F.A.S.T. catches most strokes, but not all. The American Stroke Association warns about signs that are easy to dismiss. Women often have a sudden severe headache, nausea, hiccups, or a feeling that something is wrong without a clear face or arm symptom. Younger adults can have strokes too. Vision loss in one eye, sudden severe dizziness, or trouble walking should not be brushed off. Posterior strokes affect the back of the brain. They often cause balance and vision problems instead of the classic face droop. Silent strokes show up on a CT scan with no obvious symptoms at the time. If something is sudden and severe, call 911. Even atypical strokes need the same urgent ER pathway.

Ischemic vs Hemorrhagic Stroke: Why the Difference Matters

The two types of stroke need opposite treatments. That is why the ER team moves fast to identify which one is happening. About 80% of strokes are ischemic, per MedlinePlus. A blood clot blocks an artery in the brain. If the patient arrives within 3 to 4.5 hours of symptom onset, doctors can use a clot-dissolving drug called tPA to restore blood flow. After that window, the drug can do more harm than good. The remaining strokes are hemorrhagic. A brain blood vessel ruptures and bleeds. tPA would make this worse. These patients need blood pressure control, sometimes surgery, and intensive care. A CT scan within the first hour at the ER is what tells the team which type they are dealing with.

The First 5 Minutes: Exactly What To Do

What you do in the first 5 minutes matters more than almost anything else.
  1. Call 911 immediately. Do not call a friend or search online. Just dial.
  2. Note the exact time symptoms started. Or the last time the person was definitely normal. This number decides whether tPA is on the table.
  3. Stay with them. Help them sit or lie down safely. Loosen tight clothing.
  4. Track any changes. Symptoms can worsen quickly. Tell the paramedics what changed.
  5. Do not give food, water, or medicine. Swallowing may be impaired. Anything by mouth can choke them.
Ambulances also notify the ER en route, so the stroke team is ready when you arrive.

What Not To Do: 4 Mistakes That Cost Critical Minutes

These four mistakes happen often and waste the only thing that matters: time.
  • Don't drive them yourself. An ambulance alerts the ER in advance and starts care en route. A private car arrives cold.
  • Don't give aspirin. Aspirin makes hemorrhagic strokes worse. The ER decides after the CT scan.
  • Don't wait to see if it passes. Symptoms that fade can be a TIA, or mini-stroke. About 1 in 3 TIA patients have a full stroke within a year.
  • Don't let them sleep it off. Stroke symptoms during sleep are how the time window gets missed. If you can't say when symptoms started, tPA usually isn't possible.

Stroke Risk Factors and Prevention for DFW Adults

Most strokes are preventable. The CDC lists the major risk factors, and most are within your control. High blood pressure is the single biggest risk factor. Controlling it cuts stroke risk roughly in half. Diabetes, high cholesterol, atrial fibrillation, smoking, and obesity each raise the odds on their own. Texas-specific concerns add up too:
  • Summer heat. Dehydration thickens blood and can trigger ischemic strokes in vulnerable adults. Drink water on hot days.
  • Sleep apnea. Common and underdiagnosed in DFW. Untreated sleep apnea doubles stroke risk.
  • Age over 55. Risk doubles every decade after.
What helps: regular blood pressure checks, taking prescribed medications consistently, 30 minutes of moderate exercise most days, and not smoking. Atrial fibrillation needs aggressive management because it raises stroke risk fivefold.

What Happens When You Arrive at the ER of Irving for a Suspected Stroke

At the ER of Irving, the stroke pathway starts the moment paramedics call ahead. Per NINDS stroke care guidelines, the goal is to compress every minute that matters:
  • First 15 minutes. Vital signs, blood draw, neurological exam by an ER physician.
  • Within 25 minutes. CT scan of the head to rule in or rule out bleeding.
  • Within 45 minutes. CT results read, neurologist consulted.
  • Within 60 minutes. Decision on tPA for ischemic strokes, or transfer to a comprehensive stroke center if needed.
Our 24/7 ER team is set up to keep the tPA window open. We coordinate with regional comprehensive stroke centers for cases that need endovascular thrombectomy or neurosurgery. If you suspect a stroke, call 911 and tell them to bring the patient here.

FAQs

How long after symptoms start is tPA still effective?

Up to 4.5 hours from symptom onset for most patients. Some select cases extend further. After that window, the risk of brain bleeding from tPA outweighs the benefit. Mechanical thrombectomy can extend the treatment window to 24 hours in some patients.

Can young people have strokes?

Yes. About 10 to 15% of strokes happen in adults under 50. Causes include heart conditions, blood clotting disorders, drug use, and head trauma. Sudden severe headache or vision loss in a young adult should not be dismissed.

What does a mini-stroke feel like?

A transient ischemic attack, or TIA, produces stroke-like symptoms that resolve within 24 hours, usually within an hour. The brain isn't permanently damaged, but a TIA is a strong warning sign. About 1 in 3 TIA patients have a full stroke within a year. Get evaluated.

Can stress trigger a stroke?

Chronic stress raises blood pressure and inflammation, both of which raise stroke risk. Acute emotional stress can trigger strokes in already-vulnerable adults, but it is rarely the sole cause.

What is the difference between a heart attack and a stroke?

A heart attack is a blockage in a heart artery, usually causing chest pain. A stroke is a blockage or bleed in a brain artery, causing neurological symptoms like face droop or speech trouble. Both need 911.

What is the recovery time after a stroke?

It varies. Many patients see meaningful recovery in 3 to 6 months with rehabilitation. Some have permanent deficits. The faster the initial treatment, the better the outcomes.

title.rendered: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: The Invisible Winter Threat

content.raw:
As the temperature drops and we retreat into the warmth of our homes, we naturally focus on comfort, cranking up the furnace, lighting the fireplace, or perhaps using a space heater to take the chill off. However, winter brings a hidden guest that no one invited. Carbon monoxide (CO) is often called the "silent killer" because it is a gas you cannot see, smell, or taste. According to the CDC Every year, at least 420 people in the U.S. die from accidental CO poisoning, and over 100,000 visit emergency rooms due to exposure. At ER of Irving, we believe that education is the first line of defense. Understanding how this gas behaves and how to spot the early warning signs can quite literally save your life or the life of someone you love.

What is Carbon Monoxide and Why is it the "Silent Killer"?

Carbon monoxide is a gas produced whenever you burn fuel such as gas, oil, kerosene, wood, or charcoal. Under normal circumstances, appliances like your water heater or furnace vent this gas safely outside. However, if an appliance is damaged or used incorrectly, the gas can accumulate indoors.

How Carbon Monoxide Affects Your Body

The real danger lies in how CO interacts with your blood. According to the CDC, carbon monoxide enters your lungs and hitches a ride on your red blood cells, taking the place of oxygen. Think of your red blood cells like a delivery service. Their job is to carry oxygen to your brain, heart, and vital organs. Carbon monoxide is like a "hitchhiker" that kicks the oxygen out of the seat. When you breathe in CO, your body’s tissues are starved of the oxygen they need to function. This process can happen slowly over several hours or very rapidly if levels are high, which is why understanding CO poisoning symptoms is a life-saving skill.

Dizziness and Flu-like Symptoms: Recognizing Carbon Monoxide Poisoning

The most difficult part about identifying carbon monoxide exposure is that it doesn't "feel" like poisoning at first. In fact, many people mistake the early signs for a common winter cold or the flu.

Comparing CO Poisoning to the Common Flu

If you are coming down with a virus, you might expect a fever, aches, and a cough. However, MedlinePlus (a service of the NIH) points out that CO poisoning creates a very specific "flu-like" feeling but usually without the fever. Common early symptoms include:
  • A dull, persistent headache.
  • Dizziness or lightheadedness.
  • Nausea or vomiting.
  • Shortness of breath.
  • General weakness.

Red Flags You Should Never Ignore

Because these symptoms are vague, look for patterns. Do you feel better when you leave the house and worse when you return? Does everyone in the family feel sick at the same time? Even your pets can show signs of distress, such as lethargy or unusual behavior. If multiple people in a household are experiencing CO poisoning symptoms simultaneously, you should treat it as an emergency and get to fresh air immediately.

Common Sources of Carbon Monoxide in Your Home

You don't need to be afraid of your appliances, but you do need to respect them. Most CO incidents occur because of poor maintenance or improper use of fuel-burning tools.

Heating Systems and Blocked Vents

Your furnace and water heater are the workhorses of your home in winter. If a furnace has a cracked heat exchanger or if your chimney is blocked by debris or a bird's nest, the CO that should be going outside ends up in your living room. The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) emphasizes that having your heating system professionally inspected every year is the single best way to prevent a tragedy.

The Hidden Dangers of Portable Generators

When a winter storm knocks out the power, many people reach for portable generators. While they are great for keeping the lights on, they are major producers of CO. You should never use a generator inside your home, garage, or basement even, if the doors are open. The CDC warns that generators should be kept at least 20 feet away from any window, door, or vent.

Why CO Detectors Save Lives

Since you cannot rely on your senses to detect this gas, you must rely on technology. Why CO detectors save lives is simple: they are the only way to "see" the invisible.

Where to Install Your Alarms for Maximum Protection

A single alarm in the hallway might not be enough. The U.S. Fire Administration recommends placing a CO alarm on every level of your home and, most importantly, right outside every sleeping area. If the gas builds up while you are asleep, you need an alarm loud enough to wake you up before the levels become lethal.

Maintenance Tips: Testing and Battery Replacement

A detector is only useful if it’s working.
  1. Test them monthly by pressing the test button.
  2. Change the batteries every six months (a good rule of thumb is to do this when you change your clocks for daylight savings).
  3. Check the expiration date. Most CO sensors only last 5 to 7 years. If yours is older than that, it’s time for a new one.

High-Risk Groups: Protecting the Most Vulnerable

While carbon monoxide is dangerous for everyone, some people are more sensitive to lower levels of the gas.
  • Unborn Babies: Fetal blood cells take up CO more easily than adult cells, which can be devastating for a pregnancy.
  • Infants and Children: They breathe faster than adults, meaning they inhale more gas in a shorter period.
  • Seniors and People with Heart Disease: Those with existing breathing or heart problems are much more likely to fall ill quickly when oxygen levels drop.

Oxygen Therapy in the ER: What to Expect During Treatment

If you arrive at our facility or an ER with suspected exposure, our priority is getting oxygen back into your system.

How Doctors Diagnose CO Exposure

Diagnosis usually begins with a simple blood test. We look for the level of carboxyhemoglobin (CO bound to your blood) to determine the severity of the exposure. A standard pulse oximeter (the clip placed on your finger) often cannot distinguish between oxygen and CO, so a specialized blood draw is necessary for accuracy.

Oxygen Therapy in the ER

The primary treatment for CO poisoning symptoms is oxygen therapy in the ER. By breathing in 100% pure oxygen through a mask, we can speed up the process of clearing the carbon monoxide from our blood.
  • In standard air, it takes several hours for your body to eliminate half of the CO in your system.
  • With high-flow oxygen, that time is cut significantly.
  • In very severe cases, we may use a hyperbaric oxygen chamber, which uses pressure to force oxygen into your tissues and brain even faster to prevent long-term damage.

Immediate Steps: What to Do in an Emergency

If your CO alarm goes off or you suspect a leak:
  1. Leave the house immediately. Don't stop to open windows or turn off the stove. Just get out.
  2. Call 911. Let the fire department find the source of the leak with their professional equipment.
  3. Count heads. Make sure everyone, including pets, is accounted for in the fresh air.
  4. Seek medical attention. Even if you feel "okay," low-level exposure can have lingering effects.

Prevention Checklist: A Safer Home This Winter

  • Schedule a furnace tune-up with a licensed technician.
  • Clear the vents: After a snowstorm, make sure your dryer and furnace exhaust pipes aren't buried in snow.
  • Never idle the car in the garage, even if the big door is open.
  • Use grills outside only: Never use a charcoal or gas grill inside for cooking or heat.
  • Keep generators 20 feet away from the house.

Suspect Carbon Monoxide Exposure? Get Emergency Care Immediately at the ER of Irving

Carbon monoxide poisoning can turn serious in minutes. If you or your family are experiencing headache, dizziness, nausea, or flu-like symptoms without a fever, don’t wait.

At ER of Irving , our emergency team is available 24/7 with on-site diagnostics and rapid oxygen therapy to treat carbon monoxide exposure quickly and safely.

Visit the ER of Irving now for fast relief and expert care. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (972) 893-3148

Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

Can I smell carbon monoxide if I have a gas leak? 

No. You might smell the "rotten egg" odor added to natural gas, but carbon monoxide itself is completely odorless. You can have a CO leak without any gas smell at all.

What does a CO headache feel like? 

Most patients describe it as a dull, throbbing pain that is usually felt across the forehead or the back of the head. It often gets better when you step outside into the fresh air.

If I open the windows, is it safe to use a generator inside? 

No. A generator produces as much CO as hundreds of cars. Opening windows or garage doors is not enough to keep the air safe. Keep it outdoors and far away from the house.

How long does oxygen therapy in the ER take? 

The duration depends on the severity of the poisoning. Typically, patients may receive high-flow oxygen for several hours until their blood levels return to a safe range.

Can my dog or cat get CO poisoning? 

Yes. Pets are often the first to show symptoms because they are smaller. If your pet is suddenly weak, vomiting, or acting uncoordinated, it could be a sign of a leak.

Does a smoke detector detect carbon monoxide? 

Usually, no. Unless you specifically bought a "dual" or "combination" unit, your smoke detector only looks for smoke. You need a separate carbon monoxide detector for full protection.

Can I smell carbon monoxide if I have a gas leak? 

No. You might smell the “rotten egg” odor added to natural gas, but carbon monoxide itself is completely odorless. You can have a CO leak without any gas smell at all.

Most patients describe it as a dull, throbbing pain that is usually felt across the forehead or the back of the head. It often gets better when you step outside into the fresh air.

Yes. Pets are often the first to show symptoms because they are smaller. If your pet is suddenly weak, vomiting, or acting uncoordinated, it could be a sign of a leak.

Usually, no. Unless you specifically bought a “dual” or “combination” unit, your smoke detector only looks for smoke. You need a separate carbon monoxide detector for full protection.

title.raw: Recognizing Sepsis: When an Infection Becomes Deadly
title.rendered: Recognizing Sepsis: When an Infection Becomes Deadly

content.raw:
Sepsis is a life-threatening emergency that starts with an ordinary infection. A cold, a UTI, or even a small skin scrape can set it off. The infection triggers a chain reaction that harms your own organs.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), at least 1.7 million adults in America develop sepsis each year. Most people survive when the warning signs are caught early and treated fast.

This guide covers the red flags, who is most at risk, and what to do the moment you suspect sepsis. If you already see severe symptoms, get emergency sepsis care or call 911 now.

What is Sepsis? Understanding Your Body's Extreme Response

Sepsis is not "blood poisoning" the way many people think. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) defines it as your body's extreme immune response to an infection you already have.

Normally, your immune system fights germs locally. In sepsis, that response goes into overdrive and causes inflammation through your whole body. The inflammation can damage tissue, shut down organs, and turn deadly without fast treatment.

Think of a campfire that jumps its ring and becomes a forest fire. The fire was meant to help. Now it is too large for the body to control.

Sepsis Symptoms: How to Spot the Red Flags Early

Early recognition is the single most important factor in surviving sepsis. It often looks like a "bad flu" at first. The difference is that sepsis symptoms are more intense and get worse by the hour.

The Sepsis Red-Flag Checklist

The CDC lists these warning signs. An infection plus any one of them is an emergency:

  • High heart rate or a weak pulse. As blood pressure drops, the heart pumps faster to compensate. A racing heart while you rest is a serious warning.
  • Fever, shivering, or feeling very cold. Uncontrollable shivering, called rigors, is common. Some patients instead run a very low body temperature.
  • Confusion or unusual sleepiness. The brain is not getting enough oxygen-rich blood. A person may be hard to wake or seem "not themselves."
  • Shortness of breath. MedlinePlus notes the body breathes faster to balance rising acid levels in the blood.
  • Extreme pain or discomfort. Many survivors describe it as the worst pain they have ever felt.
  • Clammy, sweaty, pale, or mottled skin. The body pulls blood away from the skin to protect vital organs.

Trust your instincts too. If you catch yourself saying "I feel like I might die" or "I have never felt this sick," take that seriously. Sepsis survivors report that exact feeling often.

Who is Most at Risk for Sepsis?

Anyone can get sepsis. The CDC reports these groups face the highest risk:

  • Adults 65 or older. Immune systems naturally weaken with age.
  • Children under age 1. Their immune systems are still developing.
  • People with weakened immune systems. This includes chemotherapy patients and people living with HIV.
  • People with chronic conditions. Diabetes, lung disease, cancer, and kidney disease all raise the risk.
  • Anyone recently hospitalized. Surgical wounds and hospital stays open the door to healthcare-associated infections.

From Infection to Emergency: How Sepsis Progresses

Sepsis usually begins with an infection in the lungs, urinary tract, gut, or skin. Pneumonia and UTIs are among the most common starting points. Trouble begins when the infection triggers a body-wide response.

Untreated sepsis can progress to septic shock. In septic shock, blood pressure drops to dangerous lows and organs like the kidneys, liver, and heart begin to shut down. That is why emergency teams call sepsis a race against time.

Why Getting to the ER Fast Matters

The risk of death rises with every hour treatment is delayed. Emergency teams treat sepsis with rapid IV antibiotics and IV fluids. The sooner they start, the better the odds.

You do not need to memorize the treatment details. You just need to get there fast. Our sepsis emergency treatment page explains what our team does the moment you arrive.

What to Do If You Suspect Sepsis

If an infection is not improving, or suddenly gets much worse, do not wait it out.

  1. Get emergency care immediately. Go to the nearest emergency room or call 911.
  2. Say the word "sepsis." Ask the provider directly, "Could this be sepsis?" That question can trigger a rapid treatment protocol.
  3. Track the timeline. Note when the shivering, confusion, or racing heart began. That timing helps the medical team.

An infection paired with a racing heart, high fever, shivering, or confusion is an emergency. Get emergency sepsis care at ER of Irving or call 911 right away.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is sepsis contagious?

No, sepsis itself is not contagious. However, the infection that triggers sepsis, like the flu, pneumonia, or a skin infection, can be passed to others.

Can you have sepsis without a fever?

Yes. While a high fever is common, some people may actually have a lower-than-normal body temperature. This happens most often in the elderly and in advanced sepsis.

What is the difference between sepsis and septicemia?

"Septicemia" is an older term for bacteria in the blood. Sepsis is the broader, more accurate term for the body's overwhelming response to any infection, whether bacterial, viral, or fungal.

How long does it take to recover from sepsis?

Recovery varies. Many people return to normal life within weeks. Some experience Post-Sepsis Syndrome, which includes muscle weakness, fatigue, and anxiety.

Can a simple cut cause sepsis?

Yes. Any opening in the skin can let bacteria enter. If a wound turns red, swollen, or painful and you start shivering or your heart races, seek help immediately.

Sepsis moves fast, but so can you. Learn the red flags, trust your gut, and act at the first sign of trouble.

title.raw: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): Signs of a Sugar Emergency
title.rendered: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): Signs of a Sugar Emergency

content.raw:
At its core, DKA is a "fuel crisis." Your body’s cells need glucose (sugar) for energy, and insulin acts like a key that lets that sugar into the cells. According to the CDC, when your body doesn't have enough insulin, sugar stays in your blood, and your cells begin to starve. To compensate, your body starts breaking down fat at a rapid rate. This produces waste products called ketones. When ketones build up too quickly, they make your blood acidic, which is toxic to your organs. While DKA is most common in people with Type 1 diabetes, the NIH notes it can also affect those with Type 2 diabetes under certain conditions, such as severe illness or infection.

Why Your Body Produces Ketones

Think of ketones as an emergency backup generator. They are fine in small amounts, but when the "generator" runs too hot for too long, the exhaust (acid) becomes dangerous. Detecting these acids early is the key to preventing a long hospital stay.

Recognizing the Red Flags: DKA Symptoms

DKA often develops slowly, but once vomiting starts, it can become life-threatening within hours. Recognizing DKA symptoms early can be the difference between a quick clinic visit and an intensive care stay.

Identifying "Fruity" Breath

One of the most distinct signs of DKA is a specific odor on the breath. This is often described as "fruity" or smelling like nail polish remover (acetone). This happens because your body is literally trying to breathe out the excess ketones. If you notice this scent along with high blood sugar, it is a definitive sign that ketones are present.

Extreme Thirst and Frequent Urination

As blood sugar levels rise, your kidneys work overtime to flush out the excess glucose. This leads to:
  • Polydipsia: An unquenchable, intense thirst.
  • Polyuria: Frequent trips to the bathroom. The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) explains that this cycle quickly leads to dehydration, which makes the blood even more acidic.

Confusion and Mental Fatigue

When your brain isn't getting the glucose it needs and is being exposed to acidic blood, you may feel "foggy," disoriented, or unusually tired. If a person with diabetes begins acting confused or struggles to stay awake, this is a late-stage symptom that requires immediate medical intervention.

Early Warning Signs vs. Late-Stage Crisis

DKA symptoms usually appear in a specific progression. Monitoring these changes can help you intervene before the situation becomes critical.
Stage Common Symptoms
Early Warning High blood sugar (over 240 mg/dL), extreme thirst, frequent urination, and dry mouth.
Mid-Stage Nausea, stomach pain, vomiting, and "fruity" smelling breath.
Late-Stage (Emergency) Rapid breathing (Kussmaul breathing), confusion, extreme weakness, and fainting.
If you have a home ketone testing kit, the CDC recommends testing your urine for ketones whenever your blood sugar is higher than 240 mg/dL.

When to Head to the Emergency Room

You should never "wait and see" if you suspect DKA. If you or a loved one are experiencing the following, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room immediately:
  1. Inability to keep liquids down: If you are vomiting and cannot keep liquids down.
  2. High Ketones: If a home urine test shows "moderate" or "large" amounts of ketones.
  3. Blood Sugar Spikes: If your blood sugar remains above 300 mg/dL despite taking supplemental insulin.
  4. Shortness of Breath: If you are breathing deeply and rapidly.

How the ER Stabilizes Blood Sugar

Walking into an ER with DKA can be overwhelming, but the medical team has a very specific, evidence-based protocol to get you back to health. According to MedlinePlus, treatment typically involves three main pillars:

1. Fluid Replacement

You will receive intravenous (IV) fluids to treat dehydration. This also helps dilute the excess sugar in your blood.

2. Electrolyte Replacement

When insulin levels are low, your electrolytes (like potassium, sodium, and chloride) can become dangerously imbalanced. These are vital for heart and muscle function, so doctors will monitor and replace them via IV.

3. Insulin Therapy

Insulin is administered intravenously to "unlock" your cells. This allows your body to stop burning fat and start using glucose again, which halts the production of ketones and returns your blood pH to a normal level.

Common Causes and Risk Factors

Why does DKA happen? Understanding the triggers can help you prevent a recurrence.
  • Infection or Illness: When you are sick (like with the flu or a urinary tract infection), your body produces hormones like adrenaline that counteract insulin.
  • Missing Insulin Doses: Forgetting a long-acting dose or having a pump malfunction is a leading cause.
  • New Diagnosis: Often, DKA is the very first sign that a person has Type 1 diabetes.
  • Heart Attack or Physical Trauma: Major physical stress can trigger the hormonal shift that leads to DKA.

Prevention: Staying Ahead of a Crisis

Living with diabetes requires vigilance, but DKA is largely preventable.
  • Check Often: Monitor your blood sugar frequently, especially when you are stressed or ill.
  • Have a "Sick Day Plan": Talk to your doctor about adjusting your insulin when you have a cold or an infection.
  • Keep Ketone Strips Handy: Always have an unexpired box of ketone testing strips in your medicine cabinet.
  • Stay Hydrated: Water helps your kidneys clear out excess sugar before it becomes a problem.

Don’t Wait: Get Immediate Care for Diabetic Ketoacidosis

If you or a loved one shows signs of DKA, such as fruity breath, vomiting, or rapid breathing, do not wait. Call 911 or get emergency DKA care at ER of Irving right away. Call us now at (972) 893-3148 for immediate assistance or to speak with a healthcare professional. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for health updates.

FAQs

Can Type 2 diabetics get DKA?

Yes. While more common in Type 1, people with Type 2 can develop "ketosis-prone" diabetes, especially during severe illness or after major surgery.

What does "fruity breath" actually smell like?

It is often compared to the smell of overripe apples or pear drops. Some people describe it as a chemical, sweet smell similar to nail polish remover.

How long does it take to recover from DKA?

With proper treatment, blood sugar and pH levels usually stabilize within 24 hours, though you may stay in the hospital for a few days for monitoring.

Can I treat DKA at home?

No. Once ketones have reached a level that causes vomiting or confusion, it is a medical emergency that requires IV fluids and professional monitoring.

Why am I breathing so fast during DKA?

This is called Kussmaul breathing. Your body is trying to eliminate the acidic carbon dioxide build-up in your blood by breathing deeply and rapidly.

title.rendered: Workplace Injuries in Las Colinas: Your Immediate Guide to Care and Recovery

content.raw:
No one starts their workday expecting to head to the emergency room. Whether you are working at a bustling construction site near Lake Carolyn or navigating a high-intensity office in the heart of the Las Colinas Urban Center, an accident can happen in the blink of an eye. When it does, the surge of adrenaline often masks pain, and the stress of "what happens next" can feel overwhelming. Understanding how to navigate a workplace injury ER Irving visit is about more than just medical treatment; it is about protecting your health, your livelihood, and your peace of mind. In Texas, the steps you take in the first hour following an accident are critical. This guide is designed to walk you through those moments with clarity and compassion, ensuring you get the care you deserve.

Why Immediate Action Matters After a Workplace Injury

When an accident happens on the clock, your first instinct might be to "tough it out" or finish your shift. However, seeking immediate medical attention is the most vital step you can take. Many internal injuries, such as concussions or internal bleeding, do not show symptoms right away. Beyond your physical health, immediate care creates a definitive medical record. According to DOL, this link between the incident and your diagnosis is the foundation of any future Workers' Compensation claim. Delaying treatment can lead to complications in both your recovery and your ability to receive benefits.

First Steps: What to Do the Moment an Injury Occurs

If you or a colleague is injured, stay calm. The following steps help stabilize the situation:

Assess the Severity and Seek Care

If the injury is life-threatening, such as heavy bleeding, loss of consciousness, or difficulty breathing, call 911 immediately. For serious but non-life-threatening injuries, have a coworker drive you to the nearest workplace injury ER in Irving. According to the NIH, quick stabilization through first aid can significantly improve long-term outcomes for traumatic injuries.

Notifying Your Employer

According to TDI, in Texas, you generally have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer. However, it is best to do this immediately. Verbal notice is a start, but a written report (email or formal incident form) provides a time-stamped record. Be specific about the time, location, and nature of the accident.

Handling Industrial Accidents in Las Colinas

The industrial and construction sectors in Irving face unique risks. From warehouse operations to infrastructure projects, "industrial accidents" often involve higher levels of trauma.

Heavy Machinery and Traumatic Injuries

Accidents involving forklifts, conveyors, or heavy tools require specialized emergency care. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) requires employers to report any work-related hospitalization or amputation within 24 hours. If you suffer a crushing injury or a deep laceration, an ER visit is non-negotiable for X-rays and infection prevention.

Exposure to Hazardous Substances

If your work involves chemicals, immediate decontamination is key. It suggests flushing the affected area with water for at least 15 minutes while help is on the way. Always try to provide the medical team with the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for the substance involved.

Common Office-Related Emergencies

Workplace injuries aren't always dramatic. In the corporate hubs of Las Colinas, "silent" injuries can be just as debilitating.

Repetitive Strain and Ergonomic Injuries
